subtopic: DEFENCE INDUSTRIES LIMITED-TRANSCONA CORDITE PLANT
DEFENCE INDUSTRIES LIMITED-TRANSCONA CORDITE PLANT
speechtext:
I should like to give the complete answer in reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) on March 29, regarding the Transcona cordite plant:
On March 29, 1943, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, considerable information was given regarding the Transcona Cordite plant-the number of employees, the total cost, ownership, use of the plant on expiration of the war, etc. The figures for the number of employees in the plant were secured by long distance telephone in order that the question oould be answered as quickly as possible an'd were given as follows: May, 1942, 4,485; March, 1943, 3,089.
Confirmation by letter of the information given by telephone later showed that the figure given for May, 1942, should have read 4,398 instead of 4,485, and the figure for March, 1943, should have read 2,961 instead 
of 3,089. Inasmuch as this question was answered on March 29, before the complete figures for the month of March had been compiled, the latest available figures were given, i.e. as of February 28, 1943. As stated above, this figure 3,089 should have been 2,961. The discrepancies as above were caused by the fact that in relaying thte figures by telephone from Defence Industries Limited to Allied War Supplies Corporation approximately 130 foremen were included in both wage and salary lists and therefore duplicated.
On April 12, 1943, in reply to a further question regarding "a proposed lay-off", a definite answer was given to the specific question, and inasmuch as monthly figures on the exact number of employees had come to hand these figures were given to the house in addition to what had been asked.
Information of this kind has to be relayed from the Transcona Cordite plant to Allied War Supplies Corporation, and thence to the department at Ottawa, and therefore some discrepancy in figures, unless all questions cover the same specific period of time, is quite understandable.
For the additional information of the house and in further reply to the question of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre of April 13, page 2197 of Hansard, the reduction from peak employment (on operations) be-< tween May, 1942, and March, 1943, as of payroll March 31, 1943, is therefore 4,398 (May, 1942) minus 2,588 (March 31, 1943) which equals 1,810.

speechtext: Is it possible for the government to obtain permission to table these? The same reply which is given here about British orders is given by members of the British House of Commons regarding their Canadian orders, because this government is involved, and it is said they cannot divulge contracts. Is there any way of getting a view of these contracts?

subtopic: ORDER IN COUNCIL EXTENDING LIFE OF DEPARTMENT OF MUNITIONS AND SUPPLY
speechtext: I do not think so. Many, in fact most of the important transactions between the Aluminum Company of Canada Limited and the British government, were made without the intervention of the Cana-dain government. It was only about a year or perhaps eighteen months ago that I was asked to become the agent of the British government in dealing with the Aluminum company. I have no record, nor has the government any record of earlier contracts which involved loans by way of capital assistance and purchases of the metal, and I do not believe it is desirable, for military reasons, to give the enemy information as to the amount of aluminum going forward each month to the United Kingdom. I ask that hon. members do not press the point because I think that the advantage to them hardly compensates for the great disadvantage to those responsible for these movements.

Munitions and Supply Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES

speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, April 16, consideration in committee of Bill No. 7, to amend the Department of Munitions and Supply Act-Mr. Howe-Mr. Bradette in the chair.
On section 7-Munitions contract.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
I will ask my colleague to move the following amendment:
That section 13 of the said act be amended by adding thereto a new subsection, to be known as subsection 4, which shall read as follows:
If the minister is satisfied, upon an examination of accounts and records of a person who has entered into a munitions contract, that the contract price paid and payable to such person contains an unreasonable profit, he may direct such person to re-negotiate the contract price and may direct that there be withheld from such person any amount of the contract price which in the opinion of the minister represents an unreasonable profit, and may direct such person to pay to the receiver general of Canada forthwith any amount which such person has received which in the opinion of the minister represents an unreasonable profit.
That subsections 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 of the said section be re-numbered 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: I so move.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Would the minister give us some indication as to what circumstances caused him to bring in this amendment? It seems to me it has some far-reaching implication.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
Before the minister
answers may I ask him in what way he has hitherto been able to handle this very difficult question. Considering the vast amount of contracts that the minister has had to handle, this point must have arisen many times, particularly so, I should imagine, in connection with contracts which have been let on target prices, where the value of the work to be done was not easily ascertainable. In these cases there was little precedent and the minister doubtless has had to proceed on a trial and error basis in arriving at a price. He must, I think, have had to deal with the difficulty in connection with which this amendment is moved.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
This is a clause giving the department power to re-negotiate any contract. The tendency is for many types of war contracts to give an increasing profit as time goes on. In repetition work the plant becomes more efficient, the workmen become more skilled, and the result is that the cost drops. It has been the practice of the department to re-
IMr. Ralston.]
negotiate these contracts very frequently. I think we hardly have a continuing contract that has not been re-negotiated two or three times and new prices fixed.
Reference has been made to target price contracts. That is a very good example. In that case the target is fixed, perhaps at too high a level, and it is necessary to revise the target frequently or to change from a target price contract to a firm price contract. We have had no great difficulty in the past in working out [DOT] these re-negotiations. Industry lias been fair and cooperative, and by mutual consent we have been able to arrange a new price level. We have the power in any event to cancel contracts, and we have the power to make new contracts, but recently we have been re-negotiating some very large contracts, and my officers believe we should have the power of re-negotiation expressly covered by the act. Therefore we are asking for it at this time.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Is it not a fact that in nearly all target contracts the minister has made provision for re-negotiation and has given himself power to raise or lower the price?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Y'es, that is true.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: That is stipulated in the contract itself?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Consequently if it is to be put into the act, it is intended henceforth to have it in the act rather than in the individual contract?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Yes. It may be both in the act and in certain individual contracts, as my hon. friend says. Target price contracts usually do provide that the minister fix the price from time to time, but this covers a great volume of contracts, such as the shipbuilding contracts, which are in process of being renegotiated, which were firm price contracts and did not contain the re-negotiation clause.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
In all friendliness and with the best spirit of cooperation, one must look at the chart issued by the department in dealing with this question of contracts. Of course these contracts must be drafted by the legal branch of the department. On the chart supplied to us, above the legal branch there is the assistant general counsel, and above the assistant general counsel there is the general counsel. The legal branch, together with these two gentlemen who belong to the legal fraternity, has been placed on the chart between the United Kingdom office and the wartime administrator, Canadian Atlantic ports. I do

Munitions and Supply Act
not think that is the right place for it. I submit that the legal branch, with the general counsel and the assistant general counsel, should be grouped with the purchase investigation branch and the munitions contracts branch. I presume the counsel of the Department of Munitions and Supply-and I apply that flattering description to all the lawyers who work there, whether big or small-prepare the contracts, and of course those contracts are supposed to be standard; I assume there are printed forms. Therefore there must be a close relation between the legal branch and the munitions contracts branch.
There should be also a close relationship between those two branches and the purchase investigation branch. After a contract is drafted by the counsel of the department I assume it is handed to the munitions contracts branch, and they must have some printed form for these contracts. Then before they agree to any contract I suppose there must be an investigation of the purchase, and the investigators are in another branch. These three branches are closely related, but on this chart they are separated, so that I do not understand how they could work very well. Of course there are many people in the department, but all those whose work has some relation to the work of another branch should be kept as close to that other branch as possible.
That is the first point I wish to make now. I suggest that the minister consider it, in order to save duplication of service. Usually the purchase investigation has to do with a deed or deeds; and while the minister is not a member of the legal fraternity, he has had enough business experience, I am sure, to appreciate that such deeds are dealt with by attorneys or solicitors. I do not see the use of the purchase investigation branch, when there is also the legal branch, and in my humble view the munitions contracts branch also should disappear, for the reason that the work supposed to be done by that branch could be covered by the legal branch. Therefore if the legal branch were put in its proper place we could dispense with the services of all the staff of the munitions contracts branch aid the purchase investigation branch. I offer that suggestion because I want to help, and to show my good spirit of cooperation.
Now I should like to say a word with regard to the new subsection 4. The minister will be given the right to say to A or B, "You have made too much money. You must pay back some of it to the receiver general." In principle I agree with that; it should be the right of the minister or any-
72537-146}
one to tell a man who has taken advantage of a contract to overcharge, that he must pay back what he obtained over what might be reasonably and justly due him. That is fair. On the other hand would it not be advisable to bring in a subamendment providing that anyone dealt with in this way should have the privilege of bringing evidence before the minister, so that his decision would not be onesided. He should have before him both sides of the picture before giving judgment in a matter which may involve a very considerable sum of money. I bring these remarks not only to the attention of the minister, but to the attention of all hon. members in the committee, so that at a later time no injustice may arise by virtue, of the amendment.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
The amendment does seem to add to the possibility of standardizing types of contracts. Members of the war expenditures committee when looking over many contracts in the past year discovered the difficulty of having contracts drawn which would merely approximate cost prices and provide for a reasonable decrease of profits. This was found particularly so in the undertaking of contracts for the manufacture of munitions, ships, and aeroplanes of novel design, in connection with which engineering practices and equipment are not well known. Computation as to costs of production in these instances is difficult.
In many such contracts there was a clause under which, notwithstanding anything otherwise stated in the contract, discretionary power was left to the minister to revise prices and profits. This applied chiefly to the target price, but to some extent it also applied to fixed prices. Hon. members may look with some misgiving upon the placing of arbitrary powers in the hands of the minister to decide what would be a fair and equitable contract. The point that worries me is that while the setting of prices and of profits may be left to the discretion of the minister, officials of his department must work with him, and it seems to me only in keeping with established practice in respect of the letting of contracts that too much authority ought not to be given to the minister and his department to overrule contractual obligations and to measure profits as he-and I do not make this observation in a personal way-according to his whims, fancies or judgment may decide.
I feel we should have some better indication of what judgment would be exercised in these cases, because one can see that it involves the difficulties with which the minister must be faced in ascertaining the efficiency of various contracting parties. An effort to
Munitions and Supply Act

increase the knowledge of the minister as to what is fair and reasonable in a given instance would mean to increase the already overburdening task of cost accountants in the Department of Munitions and Supply. I believe, too, that the scarcity of qualified cost accountants has increased difficulties in the department in connection with checking up costs of production and amounts of advances made during production.
When we embarked upon the manufacture of articles involving processes not familiar to the government or to the manufacturers a great deal of leeway of necessity had to be given. Now, however, with greater stabilization of types of production, machines, engineering efficiency and systems of checks and balances, we should operate with a much greater degree of certainty. In these circumstances I do not think the same discretion need now be placed in the hands of the minister as was placed there in the beginning. We should guard with the utmost caution and care the yardstick used by the minister and his department in reckoning costs and profits.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
The matter of profits falls into a pattern. The reasonable rate of profit depends on the rapidity of turnover, the volume used, the amount of financing done by the contractor himself, and the amount of assistance he may require from the government. All these factors are constantly being studied by the department. From time to time we get fairly clear indications that a particular profit situation is getting out of line. In such cases we ask for re-negotiations. For instance, we are making our second adjustment in respect of ships. Not only do we find that the main contractors are becoming so efficient that profits have become excessive, but we find that the subcontractors are in the same position. We have been through every main contract and subcontract in our shipbuilding programme, refixing prices. I think all hon. members agree that fixed prices which give an incentive to the builder are desirable, and we use them more and more. But even fixed prices must be subject to readjustment, or in time they will produce excessive profits.
One is amazed when he sees how costs can be brought down by organization, efficiency and repetition. To give an example, I think the first Bren gun was contracted for on a basis of $600 per gun; to-day the cost is less than $200 per gun. The first contract for rifles produced in a government-operated plant was at $80 per rifle, and that was considered reasonable. To-day I believe it is down somewhere in the neighbourhood of $25 per rifle. These are examples of the price reductions brought about by efficiency and volume. This

is a splendid development, of course. But to take advantage of the development, the government must frequently re-negotiate continuing contracts, and in fact we have been doing just that.
As has been stated, many contracts contain a clause giving us permission to re-negotiate. But we think the situation would be benefited at this time by having a general clause giving us that power in connection with all contracts.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Is it not also a fact that shortages of material's, bottlenecks, slow-downs and lay-offs have affected cost of production so much that costs of individual items have been varied from time to time, in accordance with availability of materials, of help and of engineering practices? We also have situations in which manufacturing organizations have been let contracts for certain kinds of production and who, while waiting for further supplementary contracts, and approaching a time for further financing of their original contract, have definitely slowed down their operations. Thus unit costs have increased. From this point of view I feel that any discretion left with the minister should be scrutinized carefully by the committee, as a means of safeguarding efficiency in production.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: I can say with much confidence that increased costs due to non-delivery of materials or delays in receiving new orders have been exceedingly small. So far as I can remember I have never had a claim for increased compensation based on those factors.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
I understand that a new subsection 4 is now added. The subsection now to be No. 5 contains the words:
-the contract may be adjusted or reduced to an amount which represents the cost of the work or service to be carried out or rendered under the contract.
The minister will have to be very careful because I have learned that in some cases where the warehouse or depot is not large enough there are foremen who give instructions to some of their men to sabotage some of the tools in order that all the shifts might be employed and some men get overtime. For that very selfish and uncalled-for reason they cause some of the tools to be sabotaged, and then some of the shifts would come back to work and put in time without doing any work at all. That is a serious matter. I have also been told that some business men do not count the cost but make extravagant expenditures of public money. They will make risky, experiments, and they are not afraid to do that because they rely upon the

Munitions and Supply Act
Canadian exchequer to pay for all their errors or mistakes. That is another very serious problem.
I have also been told of tanks being tested when they were incomplete and being destroyed when tested in that condition. Very often the bolts and other parts would fall out. At some plants there are proving grounds for trying out tanks.
I mention these matters to the minister so that he can have a survey made of some pf these deplorable conditions, and apply appropriate remedies in order that the best results may be obtained from the least public expenditure.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: To what extent is the cost-plus type of contract still being let, and in what particular lines of work? What measures are taken by the government to see that it gets value for the money expended in that particular type of contract?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: I think there is a misunderstanding about cost-plus contracts. The ordinary person usually thinks of a cost-plus contract as a contract involving cost plus a certain percentage, so that the greater the volume of work the greater the profit. I think there is no contract of that type in the department. We have contracts involving payment of cost plus a fixed fee. For instance, in Newfoundland it has been impossible to arrive at costs. There is a certain amount of inflation there and costs are variable and beyond the control of any department in Canada. There we have cost plus a fixed fee. A contractor is given, say, a $50,000 fee to do $2,000,000 of work. The work may cost. $1,500,000 or $2,500,000. The cost is the cost as audited by government accountants. But the fee is fixed. That type of contract is used under certain conditions where it is not possible to determine costs accurately. For the same class of work in Canada we would use the unit price contract; that is, so much a yard for moving clay, so much a yard for rock, so much for a yard of concrete in place. That is the unit price contract. The cost plus a fixed fee type we use where costs cannot be determined accurately in advance by the department or by the contractor. Where the costs can be determined in advance with reasonable accuracy, other types of contracts are used. So far as I am aware we have practically no contracts-I do not know of any, but there may be a few-of the cost plus a percentage type.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: A couple of years ago there were some contracts of that type, were there not?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: In the early days there may have been.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: When you place a contract on a cost plus a fixed fee basis, what steps are taken by the department to see that costs are kept at the proper mark, that labour is used effectively on the job, and so forth? Has the department anyone inspecting and checking the work as it goes along?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: On every contract carried on a cost basis, engineers check the efficiency of the work, and a treasury officer keeps cost records.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
Is there a standard fair
and reasonable profit on which the minister can rely in making future decisions?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
Did my hon. friend say a
printed form?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
A standard reasonable
profit.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
I dot not know that there is
a printed form but we have a certain pattern for profits, depending on a number of factors, I can say confidently that contracts of the same type are drawn to give the same rate of profit. A contract for guns would have a different rate of profit from a contract for lenses, or a contract requiring some other different technique.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: I want to bring the minister's attention to another point. Take the case of a firm that is handling some machinery shop with a yearly depreciation of fifty per cent. By reason of that depreciation the whole1 plant is eventually transferred by the government to that firm, and naturally there should be a decrease in the valuation made by the minister because of the capital that has been thus transferred to the firm. To make it) clearer, let us suppose that there is machinery' worth $1,000,000. It is being operated by a firm with depreciation of fifty per cent.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
My hon. friend's premise is
wrong. We do'.not usually allow accelerated depreciation on machinery. The government may own machinery and place it in a private plant; in that case it continues to own it and will reclaim it when its usefulness in the plant has ceased.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
Is depreciation allowed
on machinery if the machinery is supplied by the contractor himself?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
At the present time it is nob our practice to give the certificate of necessity which is required to bring a contractor
Munitions and Supply Act

before the wartime depreciation board for a purchase of machinery. The alternative is that the contractor can buy the machinery! and pay for it himself, or alternatively, the government will buy machinery, install it in the plant and continue to own it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
But when the contractor
buys it and pays for it himself, there is depreciation allowed on the machinery?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Just the normal depreciation.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
There is no possibility1
of going to the depreciation board and asking for accelerated depreciation on machinery of that kind?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: No.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
I was referring a minute
or two to leaving the discretion to the min-1 ister to renovate or renew contracts, varying them in the terms. You have the wartime! depreciation board setting accelerated deJ preciation; could we not have some sort of committee of the kind to revise contracts so far as profits are concerned, rather than leav-i ing the entire authority to the minister so to do? It is not that I am particularly fond1 of the depreciation board, because I think in some cases they have been very generous with1 their accelerated depreciation. But to adopt the suggestion I have made would be better than to leave the discretion entirely to tho minister.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: If my hon. friend suggests we should have a committee to revise contracts, it would logically follow that we should have a committee to make contracts, and from that it would follow that we would have a committee to run the Department of Munitions and Supply. I must say I am not enamoured of committees. It could be done that way, but I think the present way is better.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: I was not speaking so much of a committee as of a board, the same as the wartime depreciation board.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Committees and boards are much the same.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: May I ask again about contracts let on a cost per unit basis? Is any consideration given to the volume of the contract as related to increased efficiency in the plant? When the volume goes up and efficiency increases, who gets the advantage, the firm or the government?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
The unit prices are set through experience. The government is carrying on a great variety and volume of work. For
r\ir. Howe.]
example, take airports; I suppose the government has built 150 airports, and its officials are familiar with actual costs of airport work; they keep cost accountants on the airport to maintain the costs; not only do they know the cost and the profits on an airport which has been completed, but they have a good deal of data supplementary to that information. From that data they fix the unit price of new work, so that if the contractor is efficient he can make a reasonable profit; if he is not efficient he makes no profit or may show a loss. This has been worked out by the experience of men expert in that field who are constantly collecting new data to keep themselves informed.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Speaking of small items such as rifles, to which reference was made a moment ago; when they are let on a cost per unit basis is the specified cost per unit the same with a small contract as with a large contract?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Ordinarily we do not place that type of work in small contracts. For example, only one firm makes a rifle. When the present judge of the exchequer court was a member of the house and chairman of the committee supposed to investigate war expenditures, I asked him if he had been told by the Minister of Munitions and Supply not to put an eye on that department. He replied that he had not, and I told him not to interrupt me. No committee of the house has ever investigated the huge expenditures of the Department of Munitions and Supply. I am wondering why the public accounts committee does not drop its investigation of telephone conversations, except those made by one official to his family, and take up the whole organization of the Department of Munitions and Supply. Let the committee look into that department and give some sound advice to the minister.
Of course in these times, when incense by the ton is burned under the noses of the ministers, I am not welcomed when I speak as I do. But the Minister of Munitions and Supply is all wrong if he thinks I am prejudiced against him. On the contrary I am trying to help him, as I did on an earlier occasion when I complained about the chaotic state of his department.
When a member of the House of Commons or someone outside the house does not understand something he concludes he does not understand because the subject is profound and deep. That is why officials in the Department of Munitions and Supply are so highly praised by those who do not take the trouble to inquire into the framework of the department, and the way things are done. I am not casting any blame upon the individuals whose names I have mentioned. In their own lines they may be big business men, but outside their lines of business they have not had the experience of members of parliament. I do not know of one of these business men who would' be ready to run in an election and make the sacrifices that every one of us is making. Who is choosing these men? Were they appointed in acccrdance with an item in the estimates? No; they were the choice of an unseen hand, and that choice was approved by the Minister of Munitions and Supply. I admit that it was a great task for him to organize a department like that when he had not the human material available. But instead of dumping all branches on that chart he should have asked the coordinator of production to produce something more logical. If there is seldom logic in politics, logic on the other hand is badly needed in government.
I will go further and say that there should be a hierarchy in the Department of Munitions and Supply. The minister at the top IMr. Pouliot.]
should have in his hands the strings of all the branches, but each branch should be able to function normally without the help of the minister in all its undertakings. What I mean by that is that when the driver sitting in the cab of a locomotive turns the throttle he is not supposed to examine and inspect at every station the working of every wheel and every other bit of the machinery. That is inspected before he leaves and his engine is supposed to run smoothly. The only time he stops apart from his regular stops is when he finds or believes the machine is not working properly. But if it works well, it is not necessary for him to get out of his cab during the whole run. I am sure that I shall be blamed by some papers which receive a considerable amount of money for advertising, because I complain of the disorder that reigns in the Department of Munitions and Supply. I made the same complaint two years ago, and since then there has been no progress; it has been regress. The men there are good-natured, they do their best, but the minister cannot conceive of a plan that will work harmoniously in the production of munitions and supplies in this country. I regret it very deeply. I hope the minister wild take what I have said in the spirit in which I have said it. I have waited for two years to repeat to-day what I have said, and in saying it now I hope, sir, that if I have not opened the minister's eyes I have at least opened the eyes of some of my colleagues in this chamber.
Production is not the only question. There is also the question of distribution. What is being done with regard to distribution, we1 may ask, when we see the pile-ups of the kind I described the other day? A common' mistake in politics is to speak, only of produc-1 tion and not of distribution. A little while ago I spoke of sabotage in production. I will not say that there is sabotage in distribution beJ cause I have not proof of that, but I will sayi that the distribution of munitions and supplies in this dominion amounts to sabotage. Is it not possible to do something in regard1 to this problem of distribution? Is it not possible to cut the duplication of crown companies and branches? Is it not possible to have real control, that of parliament? I will tell you; sir, that unless that is done, disorder will not cease to grow in this country. I want order- peace, order and good government-war, order and good government-order everywhere. It is our main duty to see to it that order is established and maintained in the Department of Munitions and Supply as well as in any other department of government.

I would not say buffer. I think the time has certainly come when the government, and particularly the minister, should give some consideration to the set-up in this department to see if we cannot dispense with those who, as the hon. member for Temiscouata says, have the .final say and may be unable in vital decisions to divorce altogether their personal interests from the interests of the public which they ought in the final analysis to serve. I am not making any charge of that description, but I remember one incident that impressed itself on my mind because it came under my personal observation. One of these controllers, and he was the controller of one of the important branches, was asked in committee a number of questions intimately connected with his work and he had to defer answering until the appropriate civil servant could furnish the answers to the committee. I remember how on that occasion one member said, "If I had been in charge of that particular work for the number of months he has, I would be ashamed to admit that I did not know more about it." Therefore I think there is a great deal of justification for the criticisms which have been made this afternoon by the hon. member for Temiscouata. I have felt for the last two or three years that there was a real danger in removing these matters from parliament and placing them in the hands of controllers who have so many contacts with big business, in that by and by a group of men, not responsible either directly or indirectly to the people, may usurp the
real powers of government. No matter how careful the minister may be in this regard, he is only human, and he cannot possibly keep in touch with everything which goes on around him or control the controllers within his department. While I do not wish to say a great deal about the matter this afternoon, I believe we should pay some heed to the speech which has just been made by the hon. member for Temiscouata. After three years of the war it is altogether to be expected that younger men, who have been trained to handle the affairs of the department and subdepartments and who are not corporation officials, could take over and do the job efficiently, without there being kept in positions of influence and power men who have wide associations with corporations and businesses which may have some interests in the future of the departments and the activities of the government in many lines of endeavour.
In discussing this bill, which has such Very wide implications, and which places in the hands of the minister powers which may be called dictatorial, powers which are necessary in this time of war, powers which must be delegated to the minister at this time, we ought to see to it that he is surrounded by people who are not enmeshed in all kinds of big business and whose interests may not always coincide with the best interests of the country or further the welfare of the people.
When the house reassembles and the war appropriation measure is introduced, we should go into some of these matters very carefully indeed.

This section evidently follows to some extent the principle laid down in P.C. 4797 by which the minister was empowered to appoint investigators substantially on the same terms as proposed in this section. The powers now being given to the minister are extremely wide. Investigators are to be empowered to make certain inquiries in connection with the work of the Department of Munitions and Supply and are being clothed with extraordinary powers. I can realize, and so will the committee, that in certain instances the power given to those who are making inquiries and investigation into business affairs such as this department handles should perhaps be quite wide, but I think we have a duty to point out the possibility of such general powers in the hands of investigators being used to the public disadvantage. I do not wish to be unduly critical of the phraseology of
this particular section, but I would refer hon. members to subsection 5, dealing with offences, which reads:
Every person is guilty of an offence under this
act, who
(a)	being summoned before an investigator, fails without lawful authority or excuse to attend before the investigator at the time and place set out in the summons;
(b)	being required to produce any document or thing before the investigator, fails without lawful authority or excuse to produce the same as required;
(c)	refuses to give evidence on oath or on solemn affirmation as required by an investigator; or
(d)	refuses, when giving evidence before an investigator under this section, to answer any question which the investigator deems requisite to the full investigation of the matter into which the investigator has been appointed to examine.
Then subsection 6 reads:
No investigator shall be responsible at law for anything done by him in good faith in the performance of his duties under this section and no action shall be taken against an investigator in respect of the performance or nonperformance of his duties under this section.
In case of delegation of authority such as this from the minister to an investigator where the matters to be investigated have to do with a department of such widespread ramifications as the Department of Munitions and Supply, it can readily be seen that from the point of view of the ministry of finance and the department, wide power such as this would prima facie seem to them to be a good and proper thing. But as members of parliament scrutinizing the position which the executive take, it is our duty to call attention to the possibilities that might arise where an investigator has such very wide powers. Before I continue my remarks I should like to ask the minister this. By subsection 2, "investigator" means a person or persons appointed by the minister under this section to conduct an inquiry. Who are these investigators that the department utilizes for this purpose? And is any appeal open to anyone who is investigated who may feel that he has a grievance with respect to the conduct of the investigator and the manner in which the investigation is conducted? speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES

My remarks will be very brief, and I would have made them in committee if there had been an appropriate section in the bill itself. The Department of Munitions and Supply is, of course, the great operating business department of the war-time administration. One only needs to look at the chart, which gives a picture of the departmental activities, to realize the extent to which the government has entered through this department, into the general business connected with our war-time economy. I am not in a position at the moment, nor have I the desire, to offer any suggestions or criticisms with respect to the picture conveyed by the chart to those who desire to find out the actual set-up of the department, but in these days, when so many sections of our nation are involved in a master plan, if you like-though many of us feel that a number of factors in that master plan are still lacking-it is my opinion that in the great Department of Munitions and Supply, if one is to form an opinion from the chart which was tabled by the minister, far too little attention is paid to the position of labour in Canada. Most of us, I think, believe that in a war-time period such as this we must regard industry, agriculture, labour and all the other important sections of our national economy as part and parcel of our war-time endeavour; as a partnership, if you like. Having in mind the necessity of bringing in labour as a major partner in the war effort, it seems to me that the Department of Munitions and Supply ought to have something more in its general structure than just one official who appears as liaison officer with the Department of Labour. Labour and industry must go hand-in-hand, as two great partners in this war effort, and there must be closer relationship between industry, as represented in many instances by the Department of Munitions and Supply, and labour.
In the days which lie ahead and in the development of the Department of Munitions and Supply steps should be taken to bring into that great structure an ever closer relationship between it and Canadian labour. Speaking on third reading, I have no desire to go into details with respect to the working out
Munitions and Supply Act

of that plan. But before the final passage of the bill I did wish to raise my voice in an effort to secure a greater part and a proper partnership for labour in the operations of the Department of Munitions and Supply, and all it stands for in governmental administration.
Whatever criticisms may be made of labour from time to time, it is my view that very often a true picture is not presented. There is no reason why we should single out any part of our civilian community for either Credit or criticism. On the contrary, I should like to see every section, whether industry, agriculture or labour, taking its place as a partner in a great movement for total war in Canada. The minister should see that labour is properly represented and not lost sight of in his department. This is not the first time I have raised my voice in the house in favour of greater representation for labour and agriculture upon the various governmental administrative boards. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and others have been prone to consider my recommendation as a new theory of government. I say to them there is nothing new in that theory; it is simply a common-sense approach to a problem.
I believe that some of the greatest problems arising from our war effort can be traced to the fact that labour, agriculture and other sections of the community are not properly represented on our boards andi controlling organizations. Some of our real troubles have developed because, through lack of representation, these groups have not the confidence they should have in the boards which have been set up. In the Department of Munitions and Supply, as in other branches of government, as a nation we must not lose more time in obeying not only the letter but the spirit of the only workable arrangement through which the country can wage total war, namely, that of giving all sections proper representation in the structure of governmental administration.
As I said at the outset, I do not wish to speak at length on third reading; -but it seemed to me that at this time, with all the earnestness and seriousness I * can command I should ask the minister, before it is too late, to include in the organization of his department the partnership of labour, agriculture and those other branches of endeavour which have not been recognized to a point where their confidence is assured.

I believe the most telling statement made that morning was made by a staid, sober representative of a well-established trade union in this country. May I add my voice to what has been said by the leader of the opposition. He has repeated statements I have made since the beginning of the war to the effect that we cannot have a really democratic, all-out war effort until we bring all classes together in the organization of that effort.

Excess Profits Tax
On section 3-Revenue losses.

We have not had this bill in our hands very long. There are some far-reaching provisions in it, and I think the Chairman might read the provisions.
The explanation with regard to this section is:
This amendment gives taxpayers parity of treatment under this act and the Income War Tax Act.
Does that refer to the previous provisions of the Income War Tax Act, or to the provisions of the act which is not at present before the house?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Partly to each. I will explain what this section does. Last year we provided that with respect to businesses, a loss for the year 1942 could be carried forward and set against profits of a subsequent year, and that is one of the provisions in the Income War Tax Act to which reference is made. But this year we are providing also that farmers' losses can be carried forward for two years. Business losses can be carried forward for one year. There is to be an amendment to the Income War Tax Act to give that additional concession to farmers. These provisions, one enacted last year and one to be enacted this year, will be set out in full in the Income War Tax Act, and this is simply to incorporate that into the Excess Profits Tax Act by reference. Paragraph (d) refers to the businesses, and paragraph (r) refers to the farmers. This simply makes the same rule which is applicable to the calculation of income tax applicable to the calculation of excess profits tax.
Does this section apply the excess profits tax principle to agriculture?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It does not apply it at all. It always has applied if agriculture could have excess profits. That matter was up on the resolutions, and perhaps the hon. gentleman will remember that I said it might be that some large farmers-ranchers, for example- would pay some excess profits tax; but the great majority of farmers have earnings of less than $5,000 a year, and if they have earnings of less than $5,000 a year they are not subject to the Excess Profits Tax Act. Moreover, they are deemed to have standard profits of $5,000; the profits have to be higher than that before there would be any excess profits tax payable. Generally speaking, the Excess Profits Tax Act is of very little moment to agriculture. But it always has applied if agriculture had the excess profits. This does not make it apply.
The only reason why I raised the point was that agriculture and excess profits hardly seem to be synonymous terms.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; that is true.

I had a communication from a commercial organization in Vancouver drawing attention to the fact that some twenty-five professions were exempted under the Excess Profits Tax Act. They stated that they had written to the Minister of Finance drawing this matter to his attention. Is there any change in the act this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No; there is no change in
the act. There has been considerable pressure for changes in the act ever since it was first passed. But the provision of the act which draws a line between business on the one hand and salaried and professional persons on the other hand was drawn very carefully, after lengthy examination of the English act and their experience under it and their rules. We have always adhered to that line, although it has been a matter of grievance to certain businesses. Perhaps the most notable instance of a grievance is that of fire insurance agents, who are regarded as being businesses, while life insurance agents are regarded as not, as working on commission. That is where the line runs. Perhaps not all fire insurance agents would be on one side nor all life insurance agents on the other, but most life insurance agents are not subject to the act and most fire insurance agents are. I just instance that as a grievance. With most people there would not be very much difficulty. It is not an excess income tax; it is an excess profits tax, and a tax based1 upon the excess of incomes has many things against it. We never adopted that principle. On the other hand, excess business profits are taxed. The question is how to draw the line between business on the one hand, and non-business occupations on the other.

I.think I understand what the minister is saying. If there is a dental company, it would be subject to excess profits tax if it made the necessary profits in the period, but if a dentist were doing business on his own he would be taxed just for income tax.

speechtext:

Section 6 reads:
G. Section fifteen of the said act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"15. (1) Notwithstanding any of the provisions of this act, where the treasury board is of the opinion that the main purpose for which any transaction or transactions was or were effected (whether before or after the passing of this act) was the avoidance or reduction of liability to tax under this act, it may, if it thinks fit, direct that such adjustment shall be made as respects liability to tax under this act as it considers appropriate, so as to counteract the avoidance or reduction of liability to tax under this act, which would otherwise be effected by such transaction or transactions, and tax shall be assessed and levied accordingly and shall be payable as in this act provided.
(2)	Notwithstanding anything in this act contained, if upon examination of any transaction or transactions made directly or through the medium of third parties or by the creation of new or intermediary companies, it appears to the treasury board that any payment or benefit in cash or otherwise, received by any person subsequent to the year nineteen hundred and thirty-nine as a result of such transaction or transactions has been received directly or indirectly from a company having undistributed income on hand, then the treasury board may
[Mr. Ilsley.l
find that the main purpose of such transaction or transactions was to reduce or avoid taxation, and it shall thereupon be deemed for the purposes of this act that such person, whether he received any such payment or benefit in the form of capital or otherwise, has received income subject to tax in such year or years since 1939 and in such amount or amounts as treasury board may determine, and tax shall be assessed and levied upon such person and shall be payable as in this act provided.
Any such finding by treasury board may be made notwithstanding that such transaction or transactions may have been entered into either within or without Canada or prior or subsequent to the coming into force of this section.
(3)	Notwithstanding anything in this act contained, if substantially all of the shares of a company having undistributed income on hand have been purchased since the coming into force of this act, by any other company or companies, treasury board may find that the main purpose of the sale by the vendor was to reduce or avoid the tax which would have been paid by the shareholders of such company having undistributed income on hand on the distribution to them of the said undistributed income, and in such case, notwithstanding section four (n) of the Income AVar Tax Act, the dividends paid by the company having undistributed income on hand and received or deemed to be received by any such other company or companies shall upon being so received or deemed to be received be taxed against such company or companies and the tax shall be assessed, levied and paid as in this act provided.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I point out that subsection 1 is not in the terms of the subsection 1 that I placed on Hansard when this was under discussion in the resolutions. I have gone to the British Finance Act of 1941 to get the language for this subsection. Let me read what section 35 of the Finance Act, 1941, says:
Where the commissioners are of opinion that the'main purpose for which any transaction or transactions was or were effected (whether before or after the passing of this act) was the avoidance or reduction of liability to excess profits tax, they may, if they think fit, direct that such adjustments shall be made as respects liability to excess profits tax as they consider appropriate so as to counteract the avoidance or reduction of liability to excess profits tax which would otherwise be effected by the transaction or transactions.
The differences between that section and this are mainly these: We felt that we could not set up an outside body for dealing with these cases, that the discretionary powers are very great and that it would necessarily be a body which would to a large extent create its own jurisprudence, make its own law, and I am sure that the Canadian people would feel that we should not delegate powers under a section like that to that type of body. But the commissioners are, as decribed in the British act, a tax court, I presume, or something like that, set up under the British legislation.
I think they are ordinary citizens.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Here we have always provided that the Minister of National Revenue makes the necessary decisions in respect of taxation, and there would be an appeal from
him to the exchequer court. For one of the ministers to assume this responsibility is perhaps undesirable, because he is vitally interested in the collection of taxes. Therefore we thought it would provide an element of safety if we left the decision to the treasury board, which is a committee of the cabinet, and provided for an appeal just the same.
Are the parties allowed to be represented by counsel before the treasury board?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. There is no provision for that in the legislation, but in the one case that was heard under the section which is the predecessor of this one notice was given to the parties and they were given opportunity to appear and did appear. Their counsel did not appear but he had the right to appear and was expected to appear. For some reason, however, he thought it was better to let the parties come themselves. He did come to see me. When I was Minister of National Revenue; my colleague the Minister of National Defence was then Minister of Finance, and he was scrupulous in his provision for notice because he realized that it was only fair that notice should be given. I could not imagine the treasury board acting under any of these sections without adequate notice.
With regard to subsections 2 and 3, they are substantially the same as the ones I read before the committee. The appeal section is expanded with the view of making it clear that the Exchequer Court of Canada can correct the treasury board. This is based also on the British act. The British act reads:
3. Any person aggrieved by a direction of the commissioners under this section may appeal to the special commissioners whether on the ground that the main purpose of the transaction or transactions was not the avoidance or reduction of liability to tax or on the ground that no direction ought to have been given or that the adjustments directed to be made are inappropriate.
Our language is an adaptation of that. An appeal is already provided from assessment, and all these determinations of the treasury board lead to assessments, so that our provision reads:
(4) In any appeal from an assessment made pursuant to any finding, direction or determination of the treasury hoard under this section, the Exchequer Court of Canada shall have jurisdiction to determine whether the main purpose of the transaction or transactions or sale was the avoidance or reduction of liability to tax or whether any finding, direction, determination or adjustment ought to have been made or given, or was appropriate.
We seem to have gone as far as we can go.

When these matters
come before the exchequer court on appeal, does this section give the exchequer court power to review every part of the case which was determined by the treasury board? In other words, does the exchequer court operate to grant a blanket appeal to those who may feel aggrieved from the treasury board's ruling or assessment or levy? I want a clear and plain statement from the minister whether or not, if parties feel aggrieved with respect to a decision of the treasury board on. any of the. grounds which the treasury board dealt with, the exchequer court actually has the power under this section to revise., review and change in any way the whole decision of the. treasury board?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The powers of the. exchequer court on appeals are found in sections 58 to 69 inclusive of the Income War Tax Act. Section 66 reads:
Subject to the provisions of this act, the exchequer court shall have exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine all questions that may arise in connection with any assessment made under this act and in delivering judgment may make any order as to payment of any tax, interest or penalty or as to costs as to the said court may seem right and proper.
The proceedings in, the exchequer court on appeal may be held in camera upon request being made to the court by any party to the proceedings, and pleadings, or at least documents equivalent to pleadings, are provided for in section 63. I must say that I never participated in any appeals from assessments before the exchequer court, but they must have full power to take evidence and go into the matter. They hear a great many appeals from time to time, and I am quite sure they must have full power to go fully into all matters. They have the jurisdiction and their procedure is well settled in practice.

When discussing the resolutions of the Income War Tax Act the other evening, the minister described in some detail the difficulty in which he found himself with regard to this matter. I do not understand why the government did not adopt the procedure of having the treasury board examine the matter and, if it came to the conclusion that there had been tax avoidance or evasion, the matter could be placed before the exchequer court for a decision. Why should, the treasury board be clothed with these very wide powers when the courts of the land are available for the purpose? If the exchequer court should find that avoidance or evasion has taken place,
TMr. Ilsley.]
it would seem that the rates of taxation which had been avoided by the action of the corporation could then be applied.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This just transfers the matter to the exchequer court if there is an appeal.
Only on appeal?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, by a method that is all laid down. The procedure on appeal is laid down in the Income War Tax Act; the basis of it is the assessment, and the treasury board is given the power here to direct an assessment. Then the parties may proceed to the exchequer court, if they think that assessment is unjust under all the circumstances. I do not know that there would be any advantage in a reference to the exchequer court. As a matter of fact there would be very few cases under this section. The fact that the section is there and that there may be cases is the main thing, so that the taxpayers may take note of the section. I suppose the other method might have been followed, though it would confer on the exchequer court a new jurisdiction which it does not now have. The exchequer court has always been regarded as the appeal court in regard to an assessment, and the procedure taken here was that the treasury board should come to the conclusion that the main purpose of the transaction had been the reduction or avoidance of liability to taxation; that it should try to ascertain how much tax had been avoided or how much money had been obtained in forms other than income which really should be regarded as income. The treasury board would make these findings, and then if a party were aggrieved he could take the matter to the exchequer court.
I wish to direct the attention of hon. members to the fact that when the British went as far as they did, it indicates that they have a problem there. In my judgment, subsection 1 goes further than subsections 2 and 3. It is a more drastic subsection, and is taken almost word for word from the British act. Many people consider that in the British statutes they describe specifically what they want to legislate against, and then let a person avoid that legislation if he can. To those people it must come as a surprise to find that they gave such sweeping powers to anyone as are found in this provision, because all their commissioners have to find is that the main purpose for which the transaction or transactions was or were effected was the avoidance or reduction of liability to tax. When they find that, they may direct such adjustment

Excess Profits Tax
as they consider appropriate in order to counteract the reduction or avoidance of liability to tax which would otherwise be effected by such transaction or transactions.
Do the British have a similar section in regard to ordinary income tax or just in regard to the excess profits tax, which is quite a bit different?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know whether or not they have it in regard to ordinary income tax, but I do not see any difference in principle. They have all kinds of provisions. They enact these sections; they find that they do not operate, and they try something new. I do not know just what acts they are in, but this one is taken from the excess profits tax act.

It seems to me the suggestion I made would have this advantage, that it would be the courts of the land, instead of the treasury board, that would find guilt. I may not be correct in saying it would be the exchequer court, but it seems to me there would be great advantages in having a court as the instrument by means of which guilt is brought home to a person.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There may be nothing illegal in the transaction that is impugned, so that it is hardly correct to say that the treasury board will find any guilt. All they find is that persons may have legally entered into transactions whose main purpose was the avoidance of tax. Then they say, "That is all right; it is not an illegal transaction. The property has passed; new rights have been created, and so on, but your main purpose was the avoidance of tax, and you cannot do that to us. You have to pay us some tax there." It is not exactly a determination of guilt; it is a highly discretionary determination of the amount of tax that was avoided or the amount of income that was received in some other form, thereby avoiding taxation. Of course, if we left it to the exchequer court, what I am about to say would not apply; but if we left it to a board, I am sure all this, criticism in regard to bureaucrats and bureaucracy, the delegation of power to irresponsible bodies, and the setting up of cumbersome and expensive machinery, would break right out. If we leave it to the exchequer court in the first instance, that court has not any body of law to guide it. Of course it will have to form a body of law if there are appeals; I admit that. But I would hope that probably there would not be any appeals. I should hope that probably there would not be any cases under this.

If there is not a liability avoided, how in the world could the exchequer court decide that there was a responsibility
to pay. The minister said that in cases where the treasury board would find that taxation had been avoided by legal means, and by circumventing the taxing intentions of the act-not against any known law-treasury board must make substantive law to find a basis upon which the tax could1 be collected. That is, I take it, if we were to refer a matter to the exchequer court, that court would have to go by existing law. They could not make law, ab initio, as treasury board really has done. That is the crux of the whole situation, because in effect the minister is saying that although no law says you shall pay it, just because you have intended to form some sort of system whereby you can circumvent the law, and yet be within it, you must pay. Is that not the situation?

In my opinion subsection I is an improvement over the section in the resolutions of the Income War Tax Act. But I think the point made by the hon. member for Carleton is an important one. It is one which struck me, as I read this particular section. No matter what treasury board may find, when a case comes to the exchequer court that court will have to find within the terms of the provisions of the Excess Profits Tax Act the reasons why it should come to the conclusion that the taxpayer had avoided liability under the provisions of the act.
By legal means?

Yes. So that it seems to me this subsection is unnecessary. I was going to say that the more I think about it, and the more I consider the principle embodied in the subsection, it appears to me that it is an unwise thing for a committee of government to inject itself into the actual hurley-burley of the settlement of disputes, with the possibility of holding public hearings. It is quite true that past history has shown that there have not been many cases under the present section of the Income War Tax Act. But who can tell, with the immense broadening of taxation, that there might not be many cases arising either under the provisions of this measure, or under the Income War Tax Act.. Then we would have the example of a committee of government taking evidence, listening to complaints, weighing this and that, and then giving a decision which, if taken to the exchequer court, will be decided on the provisions of the act, other than that particular section. I suggest to the minister that if he still believes the subsection is necessary, it- might be wise to make the commissioner of income tax the person who, in the first instance, makes the finding
Excess Profits Tax

that there is an avoidance, and that it would become operative as against the taxpayer only upon being approved by treasury board. It seems to me that would impose the duty on an official of the crown who, frankly, has to do the research work in connection with investigating and considering the details of evidence. He has to do that anyway, it seems to me, and it would keep treasury board and the government as an institution out of the arena of disputes between citizens.
I do not like in any act a provision, such as that in the Income War Tax Act, whereby there is an appeal from the income tax commissioner to the minister, who is charged with the duty of reviewing the findings of the income tax commissioner. We all know that the minister cannot possibly discharge that duty. I do not believe any act passed by parliament should hold out to any citizen the assumption that the minister in his capacity as minister can go to the trouble or take the time to consider the merits of a certain taxpayer's case when, in fact, we know in actual practice that is not done.
I hesitate to see that principle extended because, if there are many cases, I do not believe treasury board could honestly and fairly discharge the duties imposed upon it by the section. Like the hon. member for Carleton, I suggest to the minister that the section will add nothing to the efficacy of the Excess Profits Tax Act; and that if, in his opinion, it does, and he considers it necessary, it would be wise to put the duty on the income tax commissioner, and have his decision operative with respect to this type of case, only with the approval of treasury board.

It seems to me that this provision in the act in effect sets up a judicial forum without actually setting up a law to be administered by that forum. In other words, it says, "You are setting up a body either to enlarge the existing law, or to modify it, and not to interpret it." But you are not giving them the basic principle of law on which they can adjudicate upon it. For that reason I go a long way with the hon. member for Swift Current; but the suggestion that the income tax commissioner should be the first person to adjudicate upon it and also originate the law still infringes that one point, even though appealable to the minister or to the exchequer court. In other words, it is a basic principle that the courts should interpret the law, not make it. They should make the law only in so far as they are interpreting existing law.
Must the commissioner of income tax not do this with all income tax returns?

No. I would say that the income tax commissioner only interprets the existing state of affairs in accordance with existing law. But the Minister of Finance has said, and I think quite truly, that he who must resort to treasury board for a decision whether he must pay tax, has not broken any law. He has not committed any offence. In the minister's own words he has not broken the law; he has not committed any offence, and yet he has to come before the commissioner or treasury board for a decision whether he must pay a tax. It should only be for treasury board to decide under what law, statute or enactment he must pay it. And he is ab initio breaking the law in avoiding it, if he should be called upon to pay.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no doubt the hon. member for Carleton is correct in theory. I am the first to admit that these are very wide powers being given to treasury board. We would not be arguing about this section at all if we could define in advance the types of avoidance resorted to. But if we were to follow the principles expressed by some hon. members, we would be legislating just a little too late in every case. All through the years we would be legislating too late.
Is that not the general situation in connection with the law, after all?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
A new type of avoidance
would be worked out. We would see it happening, and we would say, "We must not lay down a broad power to catch people like that in the future, because that is not specific enough; and we must not legislate retroactively because that is not usual." Accordingly we would just legislate to prevent it, and they would never do it again. But they would do something else. I would not be so insistent about this legislation if -it were not for the fact that we are at war. It is perfectly reasonable to ask people not to do things for the main purpose of avoiding taxation, and it is also perfectly reasonable to say, " If what you did was for the purpose of avoiding taxation, and on that point of fact you get all the appeals in the world, you should go to the Exchequer Court of Canada; it has jurisdiction to decide that fact. This is something that is going to happen to you taxwise." It must be left to somebody with wide discretion, and rather than leave it to what are called bureaucrats, irresponsible persons, it seems to me that the appropriate body is treasury board, which is a committee of the government responsible to this parliament.
Let us consider what the hon. member for Swift Current says. He suggests that we say

Excess Profits Tax
that in the first instance the commissioner of income tax shall exercise this power or make this determination, but that it shall not be effective unless approved by treasury board. That, in practice, is exactly what will be done.

I would rather have it
stated in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The commissioner of income tax will be the one who will bring to his minister a case and say: See what is happening here. If the minister considers it is a proper case he will refer it to treasury board, and treasury board will consider whether they should go further with it or not. If they decide to go further they will notify the parties and make some just and proper disposition of the case. They will do what is appropriate. Those are the words that are used here. This is not the ordinary language of statutes or of lawyers-not at all. This is something new. It is strange language to members of the legal profession.
You are giving them a lesson.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; I am not giving anybody a lesson. But they found they had to do it in Great Britain, and it is obvious that we have to do something like that. If we misuse or abuse our powers we will pay the penalty. If we are too harsh or too easy we shall pay the penalty. If we find that treasury board cannot handle it we may have to set up some body to handle it. It may be possible at some time to lay down some rules to cover it. For a great many years now we have been talking about this matter, and the commissioner of income tax has said that the devices and ingenuity which are used are so great that it is impossible to write sections which will specifically describe the state of affairs so as to result in the raising of the tax.

-What the minister says is true, but after all is there not another principle to be considered? We are in fact trying to deal with some case that may arise in the future. We are guessing at what may happen. We are not making a law to cover an offence that has already been committed but are grasping into the future, and guessing at an offence that may be committed. Before there was a law against stealing, stealing existed, and against going beyond that' principle I protest vehemently. I think we should go on the common-sense principle of passing a law to deal with an offence when it is found to exist. We must not be too progressive. We cannot entirely wipe out all our past traditions. We cannot
eradicate the past and say that we are standing up here in this nineteenth parliament and with the wisdom of Socrates and the statesmanship of Pericles passing a law to cover something that may happen in the future. We may lose something by not taxing; but when the actual situation arises, that is the time to pass a law to stop the thing, not before it is done.
I would not call this law progressive; I would call it radical. How much has the treasury of Canada lost by not having a law like this? How much money is involved?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not give any estimate, but we are in big figures in these transactions. There is nothing small about this.
How much would it be?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not give any estimate.

Under subsection 1 of the new section 15, is it the intention, if you smell a rat, shall I say, to insist on the whole transaction or series of transactions being undone? I find that the second subsection gives the treasury board power to trace the proceeds into the hands of any person who may receive them, notwithstanding the fact that they may be different from the original shareholders of the No. 1 company. Would the minister explain what is envisaged by the section which I have had a chance to read only since coming into the chamber this evening? Does he intend to undo these transactions and put everything into the status quo before the transactions were entered into.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no power here to undo transactions. There is just the power to tax the persons.

Suppose the proceeds
got into the hands of very small shareholders; you would not get your tax anyway.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Possibly not. It might be that the transaction would result in persons receiving payments, benefits in cash or otherwise, who were perfectly innocent of any intention of avoiding the tax. It might very well be that it would be an injustice to touch them at all.

But you are going to
touch them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is nothing here that
says so.

If it is not the intention to undo what has taken place, what is the good of doing anything?
