speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is simply to get taxation, to assess and levy upon the persons who received the benefits.

Tax at what rate? It
makes all the difference in the world. I read from line 40 of section 15 subsection 2:
. . . and it shall thereupon be deemed for the purposes of this act that such person-
That is the one who received the payment. -whether he received any such payment or benefit in the form of capital or otherwise, hag received income subject to tax in such year or years since 1939 and in such amount or amounts as treasury board may determine, and tax shall be assessed and levied upon such person and shall be payable as in this act provided.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The tax would depend upon the income. It says it shall be deemed that such person has received income. Once it is deemed to be part of his income, the tax goes on at the statutory rate. There is nothing arbitrary about the tax. The same principle applies in subsection 3. In the British section, which as I say is more drastic, that safeguard is not present. In subsection 1 what is directed is an adjustment as respects liability to tax which shall counteract the avoidance or reduction of liability to tax which has taken place. That is as far as the treasury board would have the right to go. You do not know the rate there until you have gone through certain computations in order to determine the liability to tax appropriate to counteract the avoidance of liability to tax. That is the language of the British section. As I say, I think we were, if anything, more circumspect in drawing sections 2 and 3 than that, but the former section 32A went, I believe, further than the British section,

The ministry do not seem to realize that there might be any significance in the statement that it is one thing to legislate along these lines for a surplus which arises through excess profits, and another thing to legislate for a surplus which arises over the course of years through ordinary business profits which have not been distributed, but which on the other hand have been ploughed back into a business in order to build it up. Morally, however, if there are any morals about this resolution, the two are on entirely different footings. I should be interested in finding out through the minister and his assistants whether there is in Great Britain at the present time any such legislation as is now before the committee. I believe all hon. members are quite willing to have any kind of legislation, whether it is against the fundamental rights of the subject versus the crown, if it is only to retrieve excess profits which this house voted unanimously against when

the Excess^ Profits Tax Act was first brought in. That is one type of profit, made out of war, sometimes referred to as "blood money", which everyone believes the government is entitled to and no one should be allowed to keep. But the legislation which will come down under the income tax act has reference to profits which were earned long before the war, and of which, I think, one is entitled to take quite a different view. I believe that is why the minister will not find any legislation in Britain having to do with anything but excess profits, when one is given such full power against the subject as is envisaged under this legislation. Therefore I should myself prefer to reserve any remarks I have to make for this legislation when it comes under the income tax act, even although it is identical in wording.
I should, however, like to ask the minister one or two questions at the present time. One is in regard to treasury board. Hon. members of this committee and the public at large have been very much concerned about the duties which are thrust upon the cabinet. We have some 10,000 or more orders in council. Let us concede that three-fourths of them are on mere matters of routine and do not require to be brought to the knowledge of hon. members. But a great many are drastic, tantamount to pieces of major legislation, embodying as they do questions of policy; and it is utterly impossible for most of us who are not members of the privy council to see how this can be done. Then a committee of the council is constituted the treasury board. That board is to be set up as a judicial body to consider intricate cases of taxation and corporate history and accounting, any one of which may easily take three or four days or a week, possibly much longer; the minister will have more experience in that matter than I have. How is it physically possible for treasury board to handle any number of cases which * may come before it? It seems to me we are designating an utterly impossible task to a body which might be fitted to perform it, but which will by no means have the necessary time in which to do so. Eor that reason I think treasury board should not be considered for this very important judicial function:	it
simply cannot perform it.
If the provision that treasury board shall determine these matters is left in the bill, what will be the result? As the acts read now, an appeal is sometimes taken from the commissioner to the Minister of Finance. To the ordinary man-and I think there is more truth than otherwise in the statement-this is simply an appeal from one man to himself; there is no real distinction.

Excess Profits Tax
Therefore it would be much better if the administration could conceive of some board or committee apart from treasury board which might more truly represent the citizens of the country and would not be interested in gathering in money for the necessary financing of the war. Such a body would be more impartial. After all, the government must get in the money; and if it sees a fruitful source, such as a case which may come before it and about which there may be some doubt, naturally it cannot help feeling that the country needs money and it must have it, whether or not justice is done to the subject. Accordingly I would again ask the ministry to consider some other board than treasury board.
In the final clause there is provision for the right of appeal. This, I believe, is quite a change from the wording of the resolution, which referred to a review of any ruling of treasury board made under the provisions of this section. The matter has already been discussed1 this evening. I wish to be absolutely sure that the exchequer court will have complete power to review on appeal the facts and any questions of law which may be involved. It is not simply a reference of certain points from the ministry to the exchequer court?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
It cannot be limited in any way?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

That is splendid.
The other great distinction between the existing and the proposed legislation has to do with the change from "no reasonable purpose is achieved by the transaction or series of transactions." That is the wording of the existing law. It has been changed to "the main purpose was to avoid taxation." None of these words are legal words, particularly; they are plain, ordinary, dictionary words, and I suppose the ordinary layman should be able to. gather their import as well as a lawyer. But it would seem that the change is made to tighten up the situation, and even though a reasonable business purpose if served, the crown, in its great dtesire and necessity to gather in revenue, will be able to set aside any reasonable business purpose. Even though the proprietor of some old firm . in one of our small towns-where there are so many-has been seeking, to gather some capital to meet his succession duties and has entered into certain transactions for that purpose, the crown will now say, "Your main purpose was to avoid taxation." The proprietor will say, "Yes, of course it was to
avoid taxation, but if I paid out all this earned surplus which was gathered by this company thirty or forty years ago, when we were building it up and creating employment for the people of the town, there would' have been little or nothing left, because the government is taking seventy or eighty per cent of my income. How can I ever get my money free to pay my succession duties?" This would seem to be a fairly rightful purpose, when the crown gets it, or a crown gets it. He is only trying to get ready for the day when he must pass off this earth; but he is never able to do so, because this fortune was left in the company when his sole purpose was not to avoid the small percentage of personal income tax which obtained throughout most of that period, but simply to use it as a business tool to build up the place and benefit the community. Now, when he realizes that old age is upon him, and he wants to get some money free to meet his obligations to the various governments under which he operates, he goes through a series of transactions, or .perhaps a simple transaction, and the crown in right of the dominion government comes in and says, "Yes, but your main purpose, even though it might have been a reasonable business purpose, was to avoid taxation.; and the whole transaction falls .by the wayside as far as any tax saving is concerned, and you must .pay the full amount of tax". So that his object is defeated. I presume there are cases like that which are covered by the change in wording from "no reasonable business purpose" to "main purpose".
Leaving that for the moment, I still believe that this committee would be fairly unanimous in approving legislation which covered cases of tax avoidance-not tax evasion, because they are clearly illegal from the beginning. It is true the minister has said that the government are not smart enough to catch up with the various dodges of artful lawyers, that they are always a step behind the parade. They cannot be very far behind, particularly when we consider that the house is sitting for five or six months or even longer each year. If one or two cases should slip by, it would not be a great loss to the crown. In the meantime the rights of the subject are protected and business men know where they stand according to the law of the land. If a particularly bad case should show up, I do not think the house would object to the passing of retroactive legislation in order to prevent a particularly big fish from getting through the net.
I suggest once again to the minister that in place of having legislation passed which so defeats the right of the subject, he should
Excess Profits Tax

have specific legislation passed to meet the cases that arise from time to time. If necessary, retroactive legislation will be conceded by most of the members of this house. That should be done, instead of having such a blanket resolution put through as he is having done at the present time. I still believe that members of this committee are entitled to know something more about the particular cases which the minister has encountered and which he has been unable to catch. He has gone back in this proposed legislation to 1939.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: It covers anything that has happened since 1939. The minister would do well to tell the committee the particulars of some of the cases. It is an important piece of legislation that we have before us. To some extent we are legislating in the dark, and from the constitutional point of view it would appear to be an extremely bad bit of law making. I ask him to consider the points I have brought up and also to be good enough to say something more about these particular cases which apparently cannot be met by specific legislation, but only by blanket legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not the particulars of any cases, but what I have heard about them in the Department of National Revenue would indicate that it would take a long time to describe the various steps and stages through which some of these transactions have gone.
Will treasury board have time to go into that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They can find time for almost anything if they have to. They have found time for a lot of things.
I should like to deal with one point raised by the hon. member for Rosedale. He mentions a case of the man who had conducted business over a period of years and, as old age approached, had a large earned surplus in the business, a large amount of undistributed income which had been piled back into the business. I am prepared to admit that the present combination of income taxes and succession duties, provincial and dominion, would make an almost impossible situation for that man. I am prepared to admit that there are some very hard cases.
The conclusion I came to was that there was necessity either for legislation or executive action of some kind, not only in one direction but in two. One direction was in the protection of the crown. We have tried to take the necessary steps by drafting the legislation before the committee. Just as soon as we get around to it we must give earnest
consideration to working out rules which will give some relief to the person who is confronted with the combination of heavy income taxes and succession duties and who has a large earned surplus or a large amount of undistributed income in his business.
We have power under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act to do that. There are cases that cry aloud for relief. I am not usually very sentimental about the griefs of the taxpayer, but these cases do offend one's sense of justice. Between now and next year we are going to try to do something, to lay down some rule of procedure under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act or work out some legislation that will provide some form of relief in some of these cases. The hon. member for Rosedale put the matter moderately enough. A man starts with $20,000 capital which he puts into a business. He carries on that business for thirty or forty years, and at the end he has $200,000 in the business, of which $180,000 is undistributed income, earned surplus.
If he dies at that stage, succession duties are payable to the province and to the dominion on an estate having a value of $200,000. In order that the executors may get money with which to pay the succession duties they will either have to wind up the company of which he was the sole or main shareholder, or declare dividends, or do something of that kind. If money comes out of the company in one year in a very large amount, it will mean that the income of his beneficiaries, let us say his widow, would be very high in that year. The tax rates are considerable, and the amount that would be left for the payment of succession duties might be quite small. It might very well be that the combination of succession duties and income tax would practically ruin the estate.
The taxation authorities recognize that; I recognize that. We have the power to relieve against that under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, but it would be a most dangerous and extraordinary power to exercise. I am simply saying that we recognize the problem. Having recognized the problem, we have to depart from the rules that apply in times when taxes are low, namely, that ordinarily no remissions shall be made. I think we shall have to make some arrangement to meet such cases. When you get your taxes very high, difficult and unprecedented problems arise, and that is why considerable discretion must be given to the taxing authorities or to the executive. To pitch this problem 'over to some outside body is pretty dangerous.

Excess Profits Tax
The hon. member for Rosedale wanted to know whether there is any provision of this kind in the income tax legislation in Great Britain as distinguished from the excess profits tax legislation. I do not know about that; I will get the information if I can when the similar section of the income tax bill comes before the house. But as was pointed out the other day, there is not the same need for it in Great Britain because they do not have anything but the individual income tax; they do not have the corporation tax in any real sense, and therefore the same problems do not arise.
I listened attentively to the hon, member's suggestion that we legislate, perhaps retroactively, for specific cases as they arise, but it is undesirable to do that to any great extent.

I am not a lawyer. Is it constitutional for us to delegate to treasury board an enlargement of our laws? In the second place, if that is done, suppose an appeal were taken to the -exchequer court and the Supreme Court of Canada; how could the supreme court uphold the treasury board without some law on which to base its decision?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This legislation gives the
exchequer court power to determine whether the main purpose is avoidance of liability to tax. There is no difficulty about that; that is a question of fact. It also gives them power to determine whether any finding, direction, etcetera, ought to have been made or given or was appropriate. That is a very odd power to give to a court or to anybody. But the reasons why we are asking for it I tried to express the other night and to-night.

This section, since it does not legislate to cover specific cases, makes one wonder what is in the mind of the revenue department. The minister has spent some time in developing the hypothetical case which I mentioned of an old resident in a small town who has been responsible for building up the industry of that place. Let me ask about a type of transaction which has not been entirely absent during recent years, and find out whether that is one of those aimed at. Is there anything iniquitous about it, because the moral line seems to be rather fine in some of these cases; some people apparently have not the right kind of moral reflex to tell whether or not something which the minister or those who will have the discretion under this section would consider something which ought to be upset? Suppose this man or company which the minister mentioned, having $20,000 original capital and over the years $180,000 of earned
surplus, ploughed back into the company, bringing about this expansion, desires to reclassify his capital stock without changing his charter or interfering with his earned surplus, and puts out a certain amount of preferred stock which he may sell to the public, perhaps distribute some common stock with it as bonus and keep the remainder himself, in that way putting himself in cash in order to meet his succession duty obligations which might come about in the near future-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: By redemption of the preferred shares?

No; supposing his company is all common stock now; he reclassifies his capital structure, has some investment dealer make an issue of preferred shares and thus gets sufficient cash to look after his obligations to the province and the dominion; is that the type of case aimed at under this section? There is no disturbance to the earned surplus, which still rests with the original corporation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know what finding the treasury board would make in a case of that kind.

Is there anything wrong with it? The trouble with legislation of this sort is that nobody knows where they stand. How is business to go ahead and make employment for people as well as carry on for the simple 'purpose of making a profit? It is quite impossible for any kind of business to be carried on unless business men know where they stand. If we are to have this type of legislation, we can be certain that business will stagnate.

We have been giving a good deal of thought to this problem. I must confess that although I do not like the wording of this section, it does something which should be done, and except for the fact that it might have been brought under an independent board or commission as suggested by the hon. member for Swift Current the other day, there seems to be no other way out than that presented to us tonight by the minister. I would, I think, go farther than this proposal goes. I should like to see a penalty clause where there is wilful evasion. I know it is difficult to prove that. The hon. member for Rosedale objects to it on a number of grounds, but if there is wilful evasion-
Avoidance. There is no evasion. That is different.

That is the distinction
the minister makes.
Excess Profits Tax

If there is avoidance which is deliberately carried out in order to escape the payment of certain dues to the government, then in my opinion that becomes evasion. It is all very well to say that if business does not know* where it stands, then legislation of this sort will affect business. I do not see why that should be so, if the business man is conducting his affairs according to the rules and legislation we have before us. If he is carrying on his business with a proper intent, then it is up to the treasury board now to prove that his main purpose was the avoidance of tax before he becomes subject to this legislation. So that personally, while I wish the phraseology could be changed, I cannot see how it can be changed and still do what the minister wants it to do.

I realize that the minister has given an interpretation of subsection 4. But I am not satisfied with that interpretation. He mentioned section 66 of the Income War Tax Act. In that there is given exclusive jurisdiction to the exchequer court; there is no limitation whatever on it. It reads:
Subject to the provisions of this act, the exchequer court shall have exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine all questions that may * arise in connection with any assessment made under this act and in delivering judgment may make any order as to payment of any tax, interest or penalty or as to costs as to the said court may seem right and proper. .
This section, in referring this matter from the treasury board to the exchequer court- and of course I must admit this is by way of appeal where in the other case it is the first time the matter has been before the court- appears to me to put a very great limitation on the jurisdiction of the court. Subsection 4 of this section reads:
In any appeal from an assessment made pursuant to any finding, direction or determination of the treasury board under this section, the Exchequer Court of Canada shall have jurisdiction to determine whether the main purpose of the transaction or transactions or sale was the avoidance or reduction of liability to tax or whether any finding, direction, determination or adjustment ought to have been made or given, or was appropriate.
All that does is to refer the matter to the exchequer court. Why would not the meaning be clearer if the last five lines were taken from the section altogether, and it read:
Any appeal from an assessment made pursuant to any finding, direction or determination of the treasury board under this section shall be to the Exchequer Court of Canada.
If the last five lines were left out, there would be no possibility of any misinterpretation in regard to the jurisdiction of the court.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not follow the hon. gentleman at all. I follow his suggestion, but I do not understand the reasoning that leads to his conclusions. To begin with, there is nothing in subsection 4 to limit the jurisdiction conferred by section 66, which gives the Exchequer Court of Canada jurisdiction to hear and determine all questions that may arise in connection with any assessment made under this act. In delivering judgment, that court may make any order as to the payment of any tax, interest or penalty, or as to costs, as to the court may seem right and proper. The point has been raised as to whether the exchequer court would have power to go back of the assessment to this direction or determination or finding of the treasury board upon which the assessment was based; would the exchequer court have power to say this? "We disagree with the treasury board. We think what they did was inappropriate. We think they did not use their discretion properly. We think the direction they gave should not have been given, the finding they made should not have been made, the determination or adjustment they made was oqe they should not have made." To clear that up, to make it plain, to put it beyond question, we have said that the Exchequer Court of Canada can do that. They can put themselves right in the position of the treasury board and say that board gave a direction it ought not to have given. Then, if that is the case, on that appeal the court can alter the assessment accordingly. If we were to do what the hon. gentleman suggests, we would leave that question still cloudy. We would not have added anything; we would have simply said that an appeal from an assessment made pursuant to a finding or direction of the treasury board lies to the Exchequer Court of Canada. Well, it lies there now. We do not get anywhere under this section until we get an assessment. The treasury board simply directs or orders an assessment, and it is no good to do what the hon. gentleman suggests, namely, to provide an appeal from the assessment, because section 66 does that now. The effect of this section is to say that on that appeal, which lies now under section 66, the Exchequer Court of Canada shall have jurisdiction to determine whether the main purpose of the transaction or transactions or sale was the avoidance or reduction of liability to tax, or whether any finding, direction, determination or adjustment ought to have been made.

It has only been a
question in my mind as to whether or not this was a limitation. The minister is definite to the effect that there is no limitation whatever in the exchequer court?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes.

Excess Profits Tax

Then I am prepared
to accept the minister's statement.

Section agreed to.
Section 7 agreed to.
On section 8-Application of section 1, of section 2, of section 3.

I did not realize that
you were carrying all of the new section 15 of the act when you did, Mr. Chairman, and if I may be allowed to do so I wish to direct the minister's attention to that part of subsection 3 of section 15 which reads:
. . . treasury board may find that the main purpose of the sale by the vendor was to reduce or avoid the tax which would have been paid by the shareholders of such company having undistributed income on hand. . . .

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Which section is that?

Lines 7 and 8 on page
4 of the bill; that section has been passed. It goes on to say, "notwithstanding section 4 (n) of the Income War Tax Act," which has . been a saving provision and, I think, a salutary one, too, under which earnings in one company which had paid the full tax to the government, and which were subsequently disbursed to and received by another Canadian corporation were free of tax in that company. Eventually, of course, the money would have to be distributed to some individuals to be used at all, and then it would come under the ordinary income tax provisions and be taxed accordingly. May I ask the minister just what the purpose is in changing this well-known provision of Canadian corporate and tax law so that it is no longer applicable. Certainly, if the surplus of the company which is disgorged, if I may use the term, goes to another company, that surplus is still intact and in corporate form and cannot be used by any person until it is finally declared in the form of dividends to individuals who have power to spend the money and who are therefore taxed when they receive it. I suppose I need not ask what the purpose is; 1 presume it is to overcome one of the subterfuges; but surely it is a radical departure from existing corporate law in this country, and I think it calls for an explanation. It seems to me that if the administration is allowed to regard any dividend which may come into another corporation under section 4(n) as taxable instead of non-taxable, as it is at the present time, we shall have considerable confusion. Of course I know the ordinary dividend from one company to another still will be non-taxable; but there may be many border-line cases, especially where any deal is involved concerning any major amount of
shares or any large distribution, particularly by companies that have not a wide public distribution, so that once more it will lead to uncertainty and business men will not know their exact position.
May I point out that where this uncertainty * exists, it is not necessarily the crown that will be the beneficiary of the policing provisions it is laying down. It means that the small business proprietor, if he has to sell, will be able to sell at a certain price to other people-^perhaps a younger generation coming along, who have money, who will not have to distribute that surplus for another thirty or forty years. The result is that the crown is no better off. The small proprietor gets a mo.dicum of the money, instead of the major portion of it. No one has any advantage except the rather sharp- if I may use that expression-promoter who buys up the old concern. And the old proprietor is then' somewhat better off than he would have been if he had distributed his surplus, and paid a tax of seventy per cent or eighty per cent on it.
Getting back to my original question, may I ask the minister why he feels it necessary to put in section 4 (n). Will it not lead to considerable confusion in J;he minds of people who have operated under that section in the past?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This section applies only to a few transactions. It applies only to cases where substantially all the shares are sold to another company. It applies only to cases where there is undistributed income on hand, and particularly it applies only to cases where the main purpose was to reduce or to avoid the taxes on the shareholders. It is expected that companies and shareholders who want to use a certain device, which is quite feasible and has been used, will take notice of that section, and not use it any more. If their purpose is a legitimate one, there is no reason in the world why, if they are thinking of moving their shares out, bodily, into another company, they cannot consult the income tax authorities, in which event they would be told whether there would be objection to it.
I gave the minister one instance a moment ago, and he could not tell me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not the income tax authority.
But the minister is the man who lays down the principles.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not the minister in charge, either-
Excess Profits Tax
He is sitting with the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -and if I were, I would be a little hesitant about reciting offhand' answers with respect to specific matters mentioned in the committee. But I do not think there is anything wrong with .that subsection.

Once again business does not know where it stands, and it must know, if it is to go ahead and! make plans. Let me give an 'illustration. Let us suppose a company has had a number of subsidiaries and put in consolidated returns but, for certain reasons, possibly taxing reasons, it decides to unconsolidate, and1 put in separate returns. There is no harm done. They paid the penalty of two per cent, because there was an advantage in taxation to them to put in a consolidated return ini the past. If they do that, it might easily be that one of the subsidiary companies, which was formerly consolidated, pays out. of its own earned surplus a substantial sum. of money to the parent company.. Surely that is quite legitimate. There is nothing surprising in that. It has been recognized right along. Yet, under a section like this, the parent company may be taxed on the income, as if the income had never really belonged to it, through the wholly-owned subsidiary which was part of the consolidation.
There are so many things involved in modern corporate practice that unless men know exactly where they stand it would seem to me we shall have chaos and confusion. So that nobody will feel that he can enter into a transaction.
Take a chance.

The minister may smile, but if he would enter into some of these transactions he would know the uncertainty with which these people are faced. Frankly, I do not understand how the minister will help business in this country, and help industrial organization unless he gives business men a body of law from which they may know their positions, and act accordingly.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943

speechtext:
Hon. ALPHONSE FOURNIER (Minister of Public Works) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize the Minister of Public Works on

behalf of His Majesty to enter into an agreement to pay to the corporation of the city of Ottawa the sum of $100,000 for the year ending July 1, 1943.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to speak at length on this measure, except again to urge that the minister set up a committee, as was suggested last year, to go into the relationship between the corporation of the city of Ottawa and the dominion government. A great deal of statistics and detail was placed on Hansard last year with respect to the condition of Ottawa as the capital city. While wartime has brought more exacting legislation to the floor of the house, yet it has brought a much more serious situation to Ottawa. Last year we dealt fully with the changed attitude in Ottawa by virtue of wartime buildings and services. We discussed the loss in taxation to Ottawa by virtue of lands being taken over by the dominion government.
There are, however, one or two greater points we might briefly emphasize to-night. Although constitutionally the government, when taking over land, is not enabled to pay taxation on it, and while under constitutional practice and law it would be improper to pay taxation on government-owned property, yet the situation as between the dominion and the city of Ottawa could, and I think should be discussed in two other respects. First of all, we must consider the greatly increased services the corporation must render to the dominion government and, in effect, to the people of Canada by virtue of the new buildings, the increased civil service and the many new services which must be rendered.
During the past winter it has been amply demonstrated that extras have been required. There have been requirements for extra street cleaning, extra fire protection, extra services, extra housing accommodation, and the many other services the city must render to the government, in return for having the capital situated here. Truly, the people of Ottawa are most appreciative of the capital city, and the presence here of the large proportion of its population directly concerned with government enterprises. But it is handicapped as well, as I pointed out last year, because, located as it is, with its great power resources, wrater communications, road communications, rail communications and manufacturing inducements, were it not for the presence here of the head of government and government buildings, it could be, and probably would be a great industrial centre. Industry has its advantages for every community.
I should like to say a few words to-night to bring before the minister in charge and the

City of Ottawa Agreement
government facts which would amply prove to them, as they did to me at least in the discussion last year, the desirability of having a committee set up to go into the whole matter, as was suggested by the member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) who was then leading the opposition, so that a businesslike and efficient system may be worked out which will adjust fairly and adequately the relations between the dominion and the corporation of Ottawa. I would not want to press this too hard at the present time; in fact I do not press it to-night, but I would urge that the matter be taken in hand at the earliest possible date.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: While I have nothing to say against the city of Ottawa and know there is no use in my trying to prevent this grant from going through, I think it is only fair to the rest of Canada to point out that over 13,000,000 a month of new money is being spent in this city by incoming war-time civil servants. By that $3,000,000 of extra money every month, the city of Ottawa was able this year to reduce its tax rate by three mills. No other city in the whole Dominion of Canada has been able to reduce its mill rate. I' cannot see where the members for Ottawa can show any extra charges that have come -upon the city. Frankly, if I had my way, the city of Ottawa would not get this $100,000 a year. It would not get one dollar, because here is the city council, with $3,000,000 extra money coming into the city every month, trying to ruin the farmers by reintroducing oleomargarine into this country. I cannot see why the people of Canada should be called upon to pay $100,000 a year to any city in war time to enable it to reduce its tax rate by three mills, and then try to reintroduce oelomargarine into the capital city of Canada.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I wish to offer a word of congratulation to the member for Carleton (Mr. Boucher). Apparently he has read and absorbed some of the remarks I made last year on the second reading of the Ottawa bill, and I am happy to say that he appears to have been converted by them. For that I am duly grateful.
There are just one or two facts I wish to point out in reply to the member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank). He will find the reasons and all the relevant data in support of this grant set out in the bound edition of the debates of this house of last year, at page 2685. May I tell him, so that he can pass it on to some of those taxpayers concerning whom he is so solicitous, that the total amount of assessment on taxable real property
in the corporation of Ottawa in the year 1942 is $146,458,368. The total amount of dominion government property, exclusive of federal district commission property, exempt from taxation by reason of the fact that it is owned by the crown, is some $61,537,700. Hon. members will see in the relationship of these two figures one to the other the reason why there is a demand for a committee to look into this question. The amount of taxes that would be paid on that tax-exempt property, were it taxable, would exceed $2,000,000 a year. I do not for a moment suggest that the proper basis is that it should be taxable, but the mere fact that it would produce a tax revenue of something over $2,000,000 will indicate the extent of the problem.
There is another aspect of the matter not generally understood. The great problem does not only arise out of the new government buildings. It arises out of the loss of revenue from buildings that were regularly paying taxes over a period of years and which have been expropriated by the crown and ceased to be taxable from that date on. In 1942 the assessed value of the taxable real estate in Ottawa expropriated by the crown was $895,475. The revenue on that item will be lost in 1943, although taxes had been paid on this property regularly in previous years.
One other item in the remarks of the hon. member for Fraser Valley that demands attention was his reference to the tax rate in Ottawa. The tax rate on real estate, when taken by itself, is not an answer. The tax rate must be taken into consideration along with the assessment, and to go into the question of assessment is practically impossible in discussing an ordinary bill before the house. It is a matter that will have to be gone into carefully in a committee. If you raise your assessment enough each year you can, of course, reduce the tax rate and still produce the the same amount of taxes.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: Did I understand the hon. member to say that you can reduce the assessment and reduce the tax rate?

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: No.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: I wish the hon. member would repeat what he said.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: What I said was that the tax mill rate taken by itself is not an indication of the financial condition of the city.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: How do you arrive at your revenue?

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext:
You must take into consideration the assessed value of your taxable property and the mill rate. The assessed

City of Ottawa Agreement

value varies each year, and to go into questions of assessment in the house on an ordinary bill is virtually impossible. The total assessment may be increased either by an increase in property values or by the assessment of new property, or by both. All this relevant information, I submit, can be gone into only by a committee set up for the purpose and having time to examine details and with authority to summons the necessary witnesses.
I stated in 1941 when a similar bill was before the house, and repeated in 1942, that the city was fully appreciative of the tremendous demands on the government for money for war purposes, and that therefore we were not unduly pressing our demands. But the situation is getting worse each year, and I had hoped that at least a committee would be set up to examine into the whole question to see if some fair and workable basis could be arrived at. I should like to urge again this year that some examining body with power to summons witnesses examine into the whole relationship between the city and the government, because many other factors that could be mentioned, if time permitted, must be taken into consideration. Having done that, the committee could recommend to the house an appropriate amount. I think it is quite apparent from any examination of the figures that the amount now granted is wholly inadequate.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: Is it not true that an increase in the population of the city and increasing business ought to increase the city's own assessment on property?

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: An increase in business will not increase the assessment on real estate. We are dealing with taxable real estate. There is an item of business assessment in addition to the assessment on real property, but it is relatively-small. I do not want to go into the whole question of assessment; I have had too much experience in municipal law trying to puzzle out the assessment act to be dogmatic about it; it is a fairly large order. I know from actual experience there are numbers of properties being sold regularly in Ottawa at prices much below the assessed values. I have in mind actual cases when I say that. I do not want anyone to draw the conclusion that the general situation is that all property is assessed at more than its actual value, but I know of many cases where property is so assessed.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext:
I think the request made by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) that a committee should be set up to go into the whole problem is a reasonable one, because none of us knows whether the amount we are voting is too much or too little,

and until a thorough inquiry is made and a fair basis arrived at, it is simply a hit-or-miss business. I regard the request as sound and reasonable.

speakeroldname: Hon. ALPHONSE FOURNIER (Minister of Public Works):
maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext:
Last year, on the discussion of the same bill, the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) suggested to the government that the whole relations between the government and the city of Ottawa should be examined by the banking and commerce committee. He complained that in committee of the whole we could not get enough information upon which to base our judgment as to the amount, whether it was sufficient or insufficient. The hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) suggested also that a committee be set up, though not the banking and commerce committee. He said: "It is still my position, and I think it only fair, that a committee should be set up to put the whole matter on an equitable basis so that the city may receive proper compensation and private taxpayers may not be required to carry an unfair burden." Some day probably a committee or some negotiating body will have to be set up as between the government and the city to see if the amount is fair and reasonable. I am glad to see that hon. members who have spoken do not wish to press this matter during war time. This would not be a war expenditure, and perhaps we would hear a good deal of criticism from outside the capital were we to increase at this time the grant from the government to the city.
This resolution is the basis of a bill to extend the life of an agreement which was entered into between the corporation and the government in 1920. At that time the amount granted to the city was $75,000. This went on for five years. In 1925 the amount was increased to $100,000 for another five years; and from 1930 on a bill was passed every year to extend the life of this agreement. Hon. members should understand that this grant of $100,000 is made in settlement -of all demands and claims of the corporation of Ottawa for the use of water for sprinkling of streets, for the use of water on the driveways and on the parks belonging to the federal district commission, and for fire protection of government buildings in the city. These are the three services rendered by the corporation for which we are paying $100,000 a year. This does not mean that the government is not expending other moneys in the city of Ottawa. Last year we voted, I believe-the amount will be found in the estimates of the finance department-the sum of $333,000 for the federal district commission.

City of Ottawa Agreement
All that money was not spent in the city of Ottawa, but it was expended in the city and the surrounding district.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: Four other constituencies.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: Yes. Some of it is disbursed in Carleton, Hull and surrounding districts. But by far the largest amount is spent in the capital city.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext:
And there is
policing?

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext:
No. We have our own force, which is the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, quite a renowned body, and sufficient for the task in the city. Last year we negotiated with the city and agreed to increase the rate for the use of water in the government buildings. If I recall correctly, we paid eighty^one or eighty-two thousand dollars for water. We also paid the taxes on the legations of Great Britain, Australia, France and other countries having legations here.
In my opinion, as the city expands and as we occupy more space here, it will be necessary to have, perhaps not a committee, but negotiations with the city, and such negotiations could well be conducted by some officials representing the government and others representing the city.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext:
Is the minister opposed
to a committee?

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: Well, at present I do not think it would be the proper means. I do not believe that at this time the government would consider increasing the grant to the city; that is, they would not wish to increase it during the war. That is the stand we have taken since 1940. Hon. members seem to agree with this point of view; and if we are not disposed to increase the amount now, the use of a committee disappears.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext:
Do not set up a
committee because they might find you should increase the grant! Is that it?

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext:
What does the minister
mean by headway?

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: That we could come to some agreement, unless the government should change its position and announce its readiness to increase the amount.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext:
I was trying to get the
situation clarified. I took it from what the minister said that the appointment of a committee would mean a decreased payment, but in the next breath he suggested that it might mean an increase. What is in the minister's mind?

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: May I point out that we are now on the resolution, and that in committee this question, may be asked of the minister and he may reply.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: I do not know what would be the findings of this committee. It wmuld depend upon the evidence produced before the committee. This request came from hon. members. So far as I recall, we have never had a request from the city for a committee. We did have a request to increase the amount; that was either in 1940 or 1941. At that time it was understood that during the war we would not consider increasing the amount. Some day, however, I believe negotiations will have to take place between the two bodies to see if the amount should be increased. I am not convinced that it shoiild be increased, but I know that hon. members from, the district would like to see it increased.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: I should like to renew the suggestion I have been making to the Minister of Public Works and the department for some time, that a number of government departments should be moved out of the city to some of the surrounding towns. According to the remarks of the mayor it would seem that some of the departments are not wanted very much in Ottawa. I urge on the government to take this action if they are to be saddled with these taxes.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: Does this amount include fire protection for the parliament buildings, the east and west blocks, the confederation building and other government buildings?

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext:
Yes.
City oj Ottawa Agreement

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: It covers fire protection services for all buildings. We have sprinkler systems in the different buildings as well as janitors.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: Does this amount not also cover a great deal of police protection? The minister mentioned other services, but he did not mention police protection.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: We have our own police in every public building in Ottawa. It does in a sense compensate for policing other government buildings where no government police are situated.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: Is not the driveway policed by the mounted police?

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext:
The federal district
commission.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: We are providing considerable police protection in Ottawa.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: I should like to point out that only a part of the driveway system is in the corporation limits.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: I regard the driveway in Ottawa as one of the most beautiful of its kind in Canada and, I believe, on the continent. I should like to know who first built this driveway and who had charge of building the Champlain bridge. Does the city of Ottawa maintain that bridge?

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: This work was started in 1899 by what was then called the Ottawa improvement commission. At that time the commission was granted an annual sum of $60,000. This grant was continued until 1909 when it was increased to $100,000, which grant continued until 1920. From 1920 on, the grant paid was $150,000, until 1925, then $200,000. In 1925 a bill was introduced to create the federal district commission, and 'there is now on the order paper a resolution to extend the life, of the commission for another ten years. At present $333,000 is paid each year for the maintenance of the driveways, parks, the grounds around the parliament buildings and different sections in the surrounding district. There are other driveways not as elaborate as the one in the city.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: In one way or another the federal government pays out $433,000 for beautifying the driveways and the federal district in and around Ottawa?

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: What does beautification mean?

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: You should know that, coming from British Columbia.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: If the parliament buildings were located in British Columbia, they would be surrounded by natural beauty and you would not have to pay for it. We buy a lot down by the old brewery and do something with it, and I.should like to know what beautification means.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: I have not the exact dictionary definition of the word, but it is to make something that does not look too well look nicer. At all events, I know what beauty is.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: Does the government pay any frontage tax or local improvement tax on pavements, roads and sidewalks in front of government properties?

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: Yes. We are subject to the local improvement taxes the same as any other ratepayer. We maintain Wellington street from Connaught place to the old Perley home, to the brewery, and the sidewalk on the north side of the street. We keep in repair the sidewalk on Elgin street as far as Laurier avenue and along the south side of Laurier avenue where it faces Cartier square.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: Do you pay frontage taxes for the frontage of the Jackson building, for example?

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext: No.

maintopic: CITY OF OTTAWA AGREEMENT AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1943
speechtext:
I think it would be a good idea to have the bill go before the banking and commerce committee where we would not only see that Ottawa got sufficient, got a square deal, but be able to' discuss the problems facing other cities in the dominion. We would be very glad to have these parliament buildings in Toronto and all that goes with them, and I do not think we would be asking for $100,000 or anything like that. We would be only too glad to get the extra revenue which would go along with them. I think the banking and commerce committee should look into this matter, and then we could take up the other public buildings across Canada. Other cities may be entitled to the same grant, although I do not think we need it in Toronto.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Fournier (Hull) thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 70,

Supply-Public Works
to authorize an agreement between His Majesty the King and the corporation of the city of Ottawa.
Motion agreed to, bill read the first and second times, considered in committee, reported, read the third time and passed.

Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence) moved that the house go into committee of supply.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee of supply, Mr. Bradette in the chair.

338. Departmental administration, $133,950.
Item stands.

The Speaker of the Senate.
110. Allowance in lieu of residence, $3,000.
I should like to know just what the senate does. Someone sent me to-night the French Hansard from the other place for April 13, seven blank pages; it seems a.waste of paper.

What about the
divorces? They work hard.
Item stands.
256. Departmental administration, $194,780.

How many departments are we going into? I understand we are not in any of these three departments up to the present. I was prepared to allow two departments to be introduced, but I do not think we should allow more than two unless there is some special reason.
I mentioned these three the last night.
I think two departments are enough to be introduced on one night.

I mentioned all these
three the other night. I do not know what ministers will be available. We are in three departments now but there is very, little chance of making much progress. The Minister of Public Works is prepared to go on with this item.

The only objection I
have is that there are so few opportunities now for hon. members to move private members' resolutions, that if we allow a number of
departments to go into supply, they can be called on Thursdays and Fridays without motion to leave the chair, and the result will be that there are no opportunities to raise matters in which members are interested.

I can only say I do not know how many votes there are; but as I remember there are seventeen or eighteen departments, and there will be only five departments in after this one is called. If we treat legislation as one there would be six, but legislation is an extra. There must be at least twenty different departments for items to be called, so that there will be plenty of opportunity for my hon. friends to debate on the motion to go into supply.
Are we going on with this?
Yes.

Since the beginning of the war, expenditures on public works have been curtailed. This year there is a decrease of some $405,351 in our estimates. We are not making any capital expenditures.
If hon. member^ will look through the esti-
[Mr. Graydon.l
mates, it will be found that they are all for maintenance, repairs, upkeep and the payment of salaries. Hon. members should understand that during the war not all properties belonging to the government come under the Department of Public Works. We have acquired some property; we have constructed some buildings. I believe the policy followed by the government at the present time is dictated by necessity. When we create a new service; when week by week and month by month that service grows and it applies to public works for space, public works has to rent premises or put up buildings. We have put up a good many temporary buildings, but we do not intend to continue forever buying properties or putting up new buildings. We think some day we- shall reach the peak and then there will be a decrease. In this city, however, we have rented nearly all the space we can find, and we bought certain properties when we found we could save money by doing so.
How do you save money by doing that?

If the rental is
so high and the purchase price is so low that we would save in the long run.

But if I may ask the
minister a question, has he not full power to take over any space on lease, just as he may take over a piece of freehold?

Yes; we can
expropriate.
How many times has the minister done that?

I have not done it since I have been in the department. Many things have been said against the public works department in the last six months, but I am there every dlay and1 I have: not seen those things happen. I have had many leases for new property. The first building in which I became interested, in connection with which tenders were being called, was the building on Sussex street for the wartime prices and trade board. It must not be thought that I am going round to the other departments telling them I can put up new buildings or rent additional space. I receive these requisitions, and have the officials make inquiries and look around. The space is not made available the day after the requisition comes in. 1 .may tell the committee that since the beginning of the war we have more than doubled the office space we occupy in this city. Speaking from recollection, I believe we were occupying 1,800.000 square feet of space before September, 1939, and we are

Supply-Public Works
now occupying about 3,800,000 square feet in this city, in addition to the space we occupy outside Ottawa.
As to policy, I would not commit the government by stating that we shall not puit up any new buildings or that we shall stop renting space. We do not know exactly what will be our future needs during this war. Every time parliament or the government decides on a new policy or a new organization we have to have space. Sometimes we do not find suitable space. I do not think this is the proper time for the discussion, but I could give a list of the properties rented in this city, and a list of properties acquired since 1939. That list would show that we have space in nearly every public building in Ottawa. We are just as anxious in the department to see a diminution in the leasing of properties, or in the erection of new buildings, but ours is not the main consideration. We have not built anything for the department; it has all been for war organizations. That is part of our work, and is taken out of our war appropriation. If hon. members will look at the break-down given by the Minister of Finance they will see that we have an amount of over $4,000,000 as a war , appropriation. That amount is outside our yearly estimates. I believe last year we expended over $7,000,000 on war projects. We are trying to keep expenses as low as we can, when they are not made in the interests of our war effort.

It may be that the minister is perfectly right in respect to the item upon which a discussion of this kind should be founded. I had in mind particularly, however, the expenditures made on temporary, war-time buildings, and the advisability of having leasehold, rather than freehold, where possible. While I am subject to correction by the minister, it has been my understanding that the Department of Public Works is the medium through which purchases of temporary, war-time buildings are made. It may be that the minister's statement respecting purchases of buildings tells only a small percentage of the whole story, one which perhaps is worse than I had originally anticipated.
I believe the minister's explanation with respect to civil estimates is one about which I cannot complain very much. But in so far as war-time expenditures are concerned, if the amount of $4,000,000 includes only a part of the expenditures which have been made in respect of public buildings and properties for temporary use during a war-time period, then
of course the story is much worse than I had anticipated, and perhaps will lead me to make further inquiries and investigations.
However, I am glad to have the minister's declaration in respect of civil expenditures. I believe it was the understanding of all hon. members that when the war broke out, the Department of Public Works committed itself to a policy of non-expenditure, so far as additional capital was concerned. What the minister has said with respect to maintenance reflects normal and proper expenditures. Concerning them I have no complaint, provided that the money spent for maintenance is well and efficiently allocated.
Is it the policy of the government, and particularly the Department of Public Works, that when properties are available for renting, at reasonable rates, or when leases may be taken over under powers conferred by the National Resources Mobilization Act, sOch avenues are first explored and all such possibilities exhausted before any scheme involving capital expenditures is entered into.

We always look over properties we can lease before we decide on new construction. We followed the policy outlined at the beginning of the war, that we would not make capital expenditures on public works for civil purposes. However, there seems to be some confusion as to the work done by the department. If hon. members will consult Votes and Proceedings of Tuesday, March 2, 1943, they will find at page 15 certain war expenditures allocated to the Department of Public Works. The amount stated is $7,096,-
000.	I believe the Minister of Finance gave a break-down of war expenditures for the coming year. While I am speaking from memory,
I believe there is an amount of some $4,000000 which will be expended in the coming year.
Civil expenditures of the department have been going down from year to year.
And of course they should.

There have been no capital expenditures made since the commencement of the war. For 1942-43 the total civil expenditures amounted to $16,533,839, in . 1941-42 they were $19,289,902; in 1940-41, $27,101,541 and in 1938-39 $21,457,824. It is clear, therefore, that civil expenditures have decreased steadily.

What is the Minister of Public Works doing to relieve the congestion in Ottawa brought about by the war, through the large number of new arrivals in the past three years? The minister's predecessor had this matter before him, and it was suggested
Supply-Public Works

that some departments might be moved to other cities, so as to relieve congestion in Ottawa, The government is erecting many temporary buildings, which are economically wasteful. After the war they will be torn down. The government is buying property in Ottawa and erecting large public buildings, some of which are for the accommodation of the armed forces. The housing situation is deplorable. The trains are filled with people who cannot find any accommodation. The minister should take a long-term view of this problem. There is a great deal of money being wasted in putting up temporary shacks to house war departments here. If one goes over the list of departments, he will find that many of them have services that relate to the large cities in Ontario and Quebec, and some of those services could be moved out of this city, resulting in an economy and more efficient administration. The minister has been in office for only a short time, but his predecessor had to report upon this subject, and I think something should be done about it. As I say, the public are coming here and cannot find any housing accommodation. Business men are complaining about this situation. The accommodation on the trains, berths and staterooms are filled by government officials located in Ottawa who could be transferred to other cities, thereby effecting a big economy and relieving the housing situation. The government is expropriating property running into millions of dollars, tearing down buildings and putting up others to house duplicate services. Rentals are very high, and something should be done about that. This matter should not be postponed from year to year because otherwise, after the war, there will be an even more serious situation in this city. Have any steps been taken along these lines since the war began? What has been done and what is the policy of the government for the next twelve months?

The public works department has no decision to take as to the location of the different departments of government. I, as Minister of Public Works, cannot tell the Minister of Finance: You should open up offices in Hull instead of in Ottawa. They know the purposes and needs of their organization, and I am no expert to tell them; you should build or rent in Toronto instead of building or renting in Ottawa. I get a requisition that office space is needed, say, in Regina. The resident architect in Regina, after being furnished with all the details as to the space required* then tries to rent the space, and the same in other cities. We are having trouble enough to house the government service without the public works department being asked to look after the housing of the public.

We have not disturbed many people in the city by the buildings we have put up or leased. We have avoided putting people out of their homes in order to erect new buildings. I have a case in mind where I objected to putting up a building on that open space at Wellington and Lyon streets, because some buildings there belong to the government and it would have meant putting some eighty-two or eighty-four people living in houses there out of their homes. We were thinking about putting up a building there to house the wartime prices and trade board, but the idea was dropped because we would have had to turn eighty or more people out of their homes.
Is the wartime prices and trade board building going up somewhere else?
We have asked for tenders.
Will it be a permanent building?
No, it will be a continuation of the national revenue building on Sussex street, down below Mackenzie avenue.
Is it a building that will be used after the war?
No; it is one of those temporary wooden buildings. We could not rent 75,000 square feet of space to house the wartime prices and trade board. There was no other solution.
I was hoping that this would not keep on.

Apparently nothing is done except to spend1 money like water on leases and buildings that are an economic waste. The government will never be able to put these buildings to any use after the war. I think the minister should explain why the dominion government does not give a grant to other cities throughout Canada in lieu of taxes on property taken over and for services given, just the same as is done in the case of Ottawa. The Ontario government pays some cities and towns a very considerable sum of money for local improvements and in connection with other matters. The minister's department has followed for thirty years this principle of paying something to the city of Ottawa for the maintenance of services for government buildings, and the same principle should be extended to other cities of Canada

Hamilton, London, and Winnipeg, for instance which have to give police, fire and many other services to the public buildings there. That is done in Australia. It is unfair that other cities

Alaska Highway
should not receive compensation in the same way as Ottawa, because the government gets these services, not at cost, but for nothing.
Does the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation look after the leasing or renting of their own buildings, or does the Department of Public Works provide them with premises?
I cannot give a definite answer at the moment, but when item 256 is reached-
That is a broad item.
Yes; I understand that, but I can give an answer then. The moment a department needs space, a lease is prepared in the public works department.

I was ejected from my
office to make room for the unemployment insurance commission.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, April 20, 1943
